title: AIP-C01 Skill 1.6.6: Chain Prompts with Bedrock Flows
html:
AIP-C01 Skill 1.6.6: Chain Prompts with Bedrock Flows

A hands-on lab building a Bedrock flow with a classifier, a condition and two prompt branches. Task 1.6, post 6 of 7.

[IMAGE: cover-1-6-6.png — alt: "Skill 1.6.6: Chaining prompts with Bedrock Flows"]

AIP-C01 Hands-on Labs · Domain 1 · Task 1.6: Implement prompt engineering strategies and governance for FM interactions · Post 6 of 7. Hands-on lab, about 30 minutes.

One prompt that handles returns, warranty claims and everything else ends up long, full of special cases, and fragile: fixing the warranty wording breaks returns. A better design splits the job. A small prompt classifies the message; a branch picks the right specialised prompt; each specialised prompt only knows its own policy. That's a prompt chain with conditional branching, and Amazon Bedrock Flows builds it without orchestration code.

What AWS says

Skill 1.6.6: Design complex prompt systems to handle sophisticated tasks with FMs (for example, by using Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows for sequential prompt chains, conditional branching based on model responses, reusable prompt components, integrated pre-processing and post-processing steps).

What it means in plain words

  • Bedrock Prompt Flows: now called Amazon Bedrock Flows. A visual (or API-defined) graph of nodes: inputs, prompts, conditions, Lambda functions, knowledge bases, agents, outputs.
  • Sequential prompt chains: the output of one prompt becomes the input of the next.
  • Conditional branching on model responses: a condition node picks the next step based on what a model returned.
  • Reusable prompt components: prompt nodes can reference a managed prompt from Prompt Management instead of an inline copy.
  • Pre- and post-processing: Lambda function nodes that clean input before a prompt (mask PII, normalise) or validate output after it.

[IMAGE: t1-6-6-flow.png — alt: "The returns-router flow: FlowInput, Classify prompt, Route condition, ReturnsAnswer, WarrantyAnswer and Handoff prompts, one output per branch"]

What we're going to do

  1. Create an IAM role the flow runs as.
  2. Define the returns-router flow in code, then prepare it, publish a version and create a live alias.
  3. Run three messages through it with tracing on, and see which branch each took.
  4. Open the same flow in the console's visual builder.

What you'll learn

  • How nodes and connections define a flow.
  • How a condition node branches on a model's output.
  • Why flows are released through versions and aliases.
  • When a flow is the right tool and when an agent is.

What you'll need

  • Time and cost: about 30 minutes, under US$0.02
  • Region: us-west-2
  • Access: Python 3.10+ with boto3; permission to create an IAM role and Bedrock flows; Amazon Nova 2 Lite through the US inference profile
  • Files: github.com/prasanth2006z/aip-c01-labs, folder domain-1/task-1.6/skill-1.6.6-flows

The lab

Step 1: The flow's role

pip install boto3
python flows_lab.py role

A flow calls models as its own IAM role, aip-lab-flow-role, trusted by bedrock.amazonaws.com and allowed to invoke Nova 2 Lite through the inference profile. IAM changes take a few seconds to apply, so wait briefly before the next step.

Step 2: Define and create the flow

A flow definition is a list of nodes and a list of connections. The interesting nodes:

Classify  (Prompt):    "Classify this customer message as exactly one lowercase word:
                        return, warranty or other. Reply with the word only."  maxTokens=5
Route     (Condition): IsReturn:   intent == "return"
                       IsWarranty: intent == "warranty"
                       default
ReturnsAnswer / WarrantyAnswer / Handoff (Prompt): one per branch

Two kinds of connection join them. Data connections carry values: the input message to Classify, Classify's answer to Route as intent, and the original message to every branch prompt. Conditional connections go from Route to the prompt for each condition. Each branch ends in its own output node.

python flows_lab.py create

The script creates the flow, prepares it (validates the graph; any wiring mistake shows up here), publishes version 1 and creates an alias live pointing to it:

export FLOW_ID=XXXXXXXXXX FLOW_ALIAS_ID=XXXXXXXXXX

Step 3: Run it

python flows_lab.py invoke

Typical output (shortened):

Customer: I opened a hedge trimmer 10 days ago and don't like it. Can I return it?
   branch: ['IsReturn']
   [ReturnsOut] Answer: ... within 14 days ... 15% restocking fee ...

Customer: My drill stopped working after 8 months. Is that covered?
   branch: ['IsWarranty']
   [WarrantyOut] Answer: ... 2-year limited warranty ...

Customer: Do you have any jobs going at your Leeds store?
   branch: ['default']
   [HandoffOut] A member of our team will get back to you within one business day ...

The branch lines come from the trace (enableTrace=True): the condition node reports which condition it satisfied. Each answer comes from a prompt that only knows its own policy, so the returns prompt can't mix in warranty terms.

Try your own message:

python flows_lab.py invoke "The blade on my HT-450 snapped after a week."

Blades aren't covered by the warranty. Does the classifier send it to warranty, and does the warranty prompt say so?

Step 4: The visual builder

In the Bedrock console, open Flows → returns-router. The same graph appears in the visual builder, and the test pane runs messages with a trace view of every node. Most teams build flows here and export the definition into source control.

Making it production-ready

  • Reusable prompts: point each prompt node at a version of a managed prompt (Skill 1.6.1) instead of inline text, so one reviewed prompt serves several flows.
  • Pre-processing: add a Lambda function node before Classify to mask PII or normalise the message.
  • Post-processing: add a Lambda node after each answer to check the format before it's returned.
  • Retrieval: replace the inline policy with a knowledge base node.
  • Release: applications call the alias. To release, publish a new version and move the alias; to roll back, move it back.

Flow or agent?

A flow follows a fixed graph you designed: right for known steps, predictable cost and easy auditing. An agent lets the model decide which tools to call and in what order: right when the steps aren't known in advance. If the exam describes a fixed classify-then-answer pipeline, it's a flow.

Common pitfalls

  • Everything goes to the default branch: the classifier added punctuation, capitals or extra words. Ask for one lowercase word, keep maxTokens small and temperature 0.
  • Prepare fails: read the validation messages; usually an unconnected input or a name mismatch between a connection and a node's input.
  • AccessDeniedException when invoking: the flow role can't invoke the model; check both the inference profile and the foundation model ARNs.
  • Editing the draft in production: applications should call an alias pointing to a version.

Clean up

  1. Delete the live alias, then the returns-router flow (Bedrock console → Flows).
  2. Delete the aip-lab-flow-role IAM role.
  3. If you kept them from earlier labs, delete the returns-assistant prompt and guardrail.

What to remember

  • Chain prompts (classify, then answer) with little code → Amazon Bedrock Flows.
  • Different prompt per detected intent → a condition node on the model's output.
  • Share reviewed prompts across flows → prompt nodes that reference Prompt Management.
  • Clean or check data around a prompt → Lambda function nodes.
  • Release and roll back → flow versions and an alias.
  • Unknown steps, model chooses tools → an agent, not a flow.

The exam scenarios for this skill are in post 7 of this task: Task 1.6 Exam Notes.

References

  • Amazon Bedrock Flows
